ex: Zero-party data is customer information that a person intentionally and proactively provides to a brand. The concept was popularized by Forrester and is generally associated with information…

b.p: Zero-party data is customer information that a person intentionally and proactively provides to a brand. The concept was popularized by Forrester and is generally associated with information customers deliberately share because they expect the brand to use it to improve their experience. Examples include a customer telling a skincare brand that they have dry skin, prefer fragrance-free products, or are looking for an anti-aging routine. A fashion customer might share their preferred clothing style, size, color preferences, or shopping occasion.

The important distinction is intent. The customer is not simply being observed. They are directly communicating information about themselves. This makes zero-party data particularly useful for zero-party data personalization. Instead of inferring that a customer likes a product because they clicked on it, a brand can use the customer's explicit preference to create a more relevant experience.

Zero-party data can include preferences, intentions, purchase requirements, product interests, lifestyle choices, communication preferences, and feedback. When collected with clear consent and used transparently, it can strengthen both personalization and customer trust.

secs.h: Zero-Party Data vs First-, Second-, and Third-Party Data

b.p: Understanding the difference between customer data types is essential for developing a modern customer data strategy.

First-party data is information a company collects directly through its own customer interactions. This can include website activity, purchase history, account information, CRM data, email engagement, and customer service interactions. First-party data is collected by the business but may be behavioral or transactional instead of explicitly provided as a preference.

Second-party data is another organization's first-party data that is shared through a direct relationship or partnership. For example, two complementary businesses may share certain audience information under an agreed commercial and privacy framework.

Third-party data is collected by external organizations and aggregated or sold for use across businesses. Its availability and role have become more limited as privacy regulations, browser restrictions, and consumer expectations have evolved.
Zero-party data is different because the customer deliberately provides the information.

The distinction between zero-party vs first-party data is especially important. A customer purchasing running shoes gives a brand transactional first-party data. If that customer tells the brand, "I prefer lightweight shoes for long-distance running," that is zero-party data. The two can work together. First-party data can show what customers did, while zero-party data can help explain what customers want.

secs.h: How Zero-Party Data Works in D2C eCommerce

b.p: In D2C eCommerce, zero-party data typically becomes part of the customer profile and personalization process. A customer may interact with a product finder, preference center, quiz, survey, loyalty program, onboarding flow, or account profile. The information they provide can then be connected to their customer identity and used across relevant Digital CX touchpoints.

For example, a beauty brand could ask a customer about skin concerns, product preferences, ingredient sensitivities, and desired outcomes. The answers can influence product recommendations, content, email campaigns, and future shopping experiences.
The process can be summarized as:
Customer shares preference → brand captures consented data → preference is connected to customer profile → personalization engine uses the information → customer receives more relevant experience.

The value increases when the information is available across channels. A preference captured on a website can potentially inform email, loyalty experiences, customer service, product recommendations, and other omnichannel personalization activities.

secs.h: How D2C Brands Collect Zero-Party Data

b.p: Effective zero-party data collection should feel useful, not intrusive. Customers are more likely to provide information when they understand why the brand is asking and what benefit they will receive. Interactive quizzes are one common approach. A customer may answer several questions and receive personalized recommendations at the end. Product finders work similarly by connecting customer needs to suitable products.

Preference centers are another valuable method. Customers can actively select interests, product categories, communication preferences, frequency, and other settings. Surveys and post-purchase questions can also generate valuable insights. A brand might ask why a customer purchased a product, what they expect from it, or what products they would like to see in the future.

Loyalty programs provide another opportunity. Members can voluntarily share preferences in exchange for more relevant rewards, offers, recommendations, or experiences. The strongest collection experiences provide immediate value. Instead of asking customers to provide information simply because the company wants data, brands should demonstrate how the information improves the customer's experience.

secs.h: How to Use Zero-Party Data for Personalization

b.p: The primary advantage of zero-party data is its ability to support more precise customer personalization. A D2C brand can use explicit preferences to personalize product recommendations, website content, email campaigns, promotions, merchandising, and customer journeys.

For example, an apparel brand can use declared style preferences to prioritize relevant products. A nutrition brand can use customer goals and dietary preferences to recommend suitable products. A home brand can ask customers about room type and design preferences before presenting products.

Zero-party data can also improve segmentation. Instead of relying exclusively on demographic or behavioral segments, brands can create groups based on customer-declared needs and preferences. This enables a shift from generic personalization to customer-driven personalization. The customer helps define the experience instead of the brand relying entirely on assumptions.

secs.h: Benefits of Zero-Party Data for D2C eCommerce

b.p: Zero-party data can create value across acquisition, conversion, retention, and customer experience. The first benefit is more relevant personalization. Explicit customer preferences can make product recommendations and marketing messages more aligned with actual needs.
It can also improve customer experience. When customers receive relevant content instead of generic messaging, interactions can become more useful and less repetitive.
Another benefit is stronger customer trust. Transparent, consent-based data collection gives customers greater visibility into what information they are sharing and why.

Zero-party data can also support customer retention. When a brand understands customer preferences, it can create more relevant follow-up experiences, recommendations, loyalty benefits, and repeat-purchase journeys. Over time, these improvements can contribute to stronger engagement, repeat purchases, and customer lifetime value.

Privacy is central to the value of zero-party data. Customers should understand what information is being collected, why it is being collected, and how it will be used. Consent should be clear, meaningful, and aligned with applicable privacy requirements.

A privacy-first approach does not mean collecting as much information as possible. It means collecting information that has a clear purpose and delivering a meaningful customer benefit in return. Brands should also avoid treating customer preferences as permanent assumptions. Preferences can change. Customers should have opportunities to update or remove information through preference centers and account settings.
This creates a more transparent relationship in which data collection supports customer values instead of simply supporting business objectives.

secs.h: Zero-Party Data Use Cases for D2C Brands

b.p: Zero-party data can be applied throughout the customer journey.One major use case is personalized product recommendations. Customer preferences can help recommendation engines identify products that better match declared needs.

Another is personalized content. A brand can tailor educational content, buying guides, product information, and promotional messages around the customer's interests.Zero-party data can also support loyalty programs. Brands can use declared preferences to make rewards, offers, and member experiences more relevant.

For customer retention, preference data can inform replenishment reminders, cross-sell recommendations, product education, and post-purchase communication.It can also improve customer service. When relevant customer preferences are available through a unified customer profile, service teams can have greater context when assisting customers.

secs.h: Zero-Party Data Strategy: How to Build an Effective Framework

b.p: A successful zero-party data strategy starts with business and customer value instead of data collection volume. First, identify which customer decisions or preferences would genuinely improve the experience. Then determine where those preferences can naturally be collected.

The next step is to establish how information will be stored and connected. A CRM, customer data platform (CDP), or other customer data infrastructure can help create unified customer profiles across interactions. Brands should then define how preference data will activate personalization. This might include product recommendations, segmentation, email personalization, website experiences, loyalty programs, or customer service.

Finally, establish governance around consent, privacy, data quality, access, and preference management. The goal is not to create the largest customer profile, it is to create a useful, accurate, permission-based profile that enables better Digital CX.

Zero-party data is valuable, but collecting it effectively requires careful execution. The first challenge is participation. Customers may not provide information if questions are too long, irrelevant, or disconnected from an immediate benefit. Data quality can also become an issue. Customers may provide incomplete or outdated preferences. Brands need mechanisms that allow customers to update their information over time.
Another challenge is integration. Preference information collected through quizzes or forms is only useful at scale when it can connect to customer profiles and downstream personalization systems.

There is also a risk of over-personalization. Using every available preference in every interaction can make experiences feel intrusive. Brands should use customer information selectively and in context.

Behavioral personalization relies on signals such as pages viewed, products clicked, searches performed, purchase history, and engagement patterns. Zero-party personalization relies on information the customer deliberately provides.

Neither approach needs to replace the other. Behavioral data can reveal what a customer is doing, while zero-party data can provide context about what the customer wants. Combining both can create stronger customer insights.

For example, a customer may repeatedly browse premium running shoes. Behavioral data identifies the interest. A preference quiz may reveal that the customer prioritizes lightweight construction for marathon training. Together, these signals can produce a more relevant recommendation. The strongest D2C personalization strategies therefore combine explicit customer preferences with behavioral and transactional data while maintaining appropriate privacy controls.

secs.h: The Future of Zero-Party Data in D2C eCommerce

b.p: As customers become more conscious of privacy and brands seek more reliable personalization signals, zero-party data is likely to become an important component of customer data strategies. The future will not simply involve collecting more preference data. It will involve creating better value exchanges.

AI-powered personalization, recommendation engines, customer data platforms, and real-time Digital CX systems can make customer preferences more actionable. Instead of collecting a preference once and storing it in a static database, brands can use it as part of a continuously evolving customer profile.

Preference-based experiences can also become more conversational. Customers may tell brands what they need through guided shopping experiences instead of navigating large product catalogs themselves. The underlying principle remains simple: personalization becomes more useful when brands understand customer intent instead of relying entirely on assumptions.

secs.h: How to Measure the Impact of Zero-Party Data

b.p: Measuring zero-party data requires connecting data collection to customer and business outcomes. Brands can evaluate participation rates for quizzes, surveys, preference centers, and other collection experiences. They can then measure whether customers who provide preferences experience better engagement or conversion outcomes. Relevant metrics can include conversion rate, click-through rate, average order value, repeat purchase rate, customer retention, product recommendation engagement, and customer lifetime value.

Experience metrics can also be important. Brands can examine whether personalization improves customer satisfaction, relevance, engagement, or perceived usefulness. The objective is to move beyond measuring how much data is collected. A better question is whether customer preference data produces measurable improvements in the Digital CX and commercial performance.

secs.h: Zero-Party Data Best Practices for D2C Brands

b.p: The best zero-party data programs follow a few fundamental principles.
Make the value exchange clear. Tell customers why a question is being asked and how their answer will improve their experience.
Ask progressively. Do not overwhelm customers with a long questionnaire. Collect useful information at appropriate moments across the journey.
Use explicit preferences carefully. A customer preference should improve relevance, not become an excuse for excessive personalization.
Keep profiles current. Give customers simple ways to update their preferences and communication choices.
Connect data across the customer journey. Preference data becomes more valuable when relevant teams and systems can use it consistently.
Prioritize consent and transparency. Privacy should be part of the customer experience, not an afterthought.

secs.h: Conclusion: Turn Customer Preferences Into Better D2C Experiences

b.p: Zero-party data gives D2C brands an opportunity to build personalization around what customers explicitly say they want instead of relying entirely on inferred behavior. When customers share their preferences through quizzes, surveys, preference centers, loyalty programs, and other experiences, brands can turn those signals into more relevant product recommendations, content, offers, and customer journeys.

The real value of zero-party data in eCommerce is therefore not the data itself. It is what brands do with it. A strong zero-party data strategy connects customer preferences with customer profiles, personalization systems, consent management, and measurable business outcomes. When combined with first-party, behavioral, and transactional data, it can help create a more relevant, transparent, and privacy-conscious Digital CX.
For D2C brands, the opportunity is straightforward: ask customers what they want, respect what they share, and use those preferences to make every relevant interaction more useful.
